title: Supersmart?
hook: The smartest person in the room may still lose to the person who breaks the problem apart.
counterintuition: Ylva expects raw intelligence to carry the forecast. The real advantage comes from decomposition, base rates, and the nerve to attack your first answer.
tryThisNow: Open a note, write one forecast you already believe about a complex decision, add a percent and a check date, then write what would make you move the number down.
keyTakeaway: Do not worship brainpower; break the question into parts, start from comparable cases, test your favorite answer, and revise when a subquestion pushes back.

breakdown.fastRead:
At 6:31 p.m., Ylva draws four boxes around the promotion forecast. The boss wants one answer. The boxes show four different bets hiding inside it. He wants the clean answer now. The paper in front of him will not give it.

Write the odds where the room can see them. Add the date, the question, and the sign that would make you change your mind. Intelligence helps most after the problem has been cut small enough to bite.

A forecast gets useful when it can be checked later. Confidence without a receipt is only weather in someone else's voice. Keep the receipt.
breakdown.deepRead:
At 9:50 a.m., Iskra, a hospital scheduler, splits a surgery backlog forecast by surgeon and ward. The average hides the part that will break first. The easy move is to pick the story that feels whole. The better move is to slow down long enough to ask what the record says before this case arrived.

A number is not a costume for certainty. It is a handle. You can move it when the facts move. You can also leave it alone when the new fact is only loud. A base rate is not a cage. It is the floor you stand on before you jump.

Picture Bode opening last year’s summer-camp numbers before guessing this year’s enrollment. The choice is not between swagger and silence. The choice is between a claim that can learn and a claim that can only defend itself.

Use the smallest clean question you can write. Put a date on it. Start from the outside view, the rate for cases like this one, then adjust for what is truly different here. Stop when you can explain the move in plain words.

A limit stays in view. Some events are too tangled, too far out, or too hidden for a sharp answer. The skill is not pretending fog is glass. The skill is knowing when the glass is only dirty enough to wipe.
breakdown.fullRead:
At 11:07 p.m., Chandra, a chess coach, studies a student's brilliant but fragile tournament prediction. She asks him to write what would make his favorite line fail. Everyone at the table can feel the pull of a clean story. It lowers stress. It gives the next meeting a script. It also hides the weak joint in the forecast, the part nobody will remember to test unless someone writes it down now.

Hand the room a sharper question. Do not ask whether the whole future will go well. Ask whether a named event will happen by a named date. Ask what would count as yes. Ask what rate similar cases have shown before. The room may groan, because the work feels smaller. The smaller work is the point. It gives reality a place to answer.

A forecaster earns trust by leaving tracks. The first track is the base rate. Before you explain why this case is special, look at how often cases like it have turned out that way. The second track is the update. If a new fact arrives, move the odds by the strength of that fact, not by the size of the feeling it creates. The third track is the review. When the result lands, save the old number and ask which assumption broke.

At 2:42 p.m., Safiya, a food-bank director, estimates holiday demand by family size, school closure, and bus route. The parts make the total less grand and more useful. This is where the craft starts to feel almost physical. The pen pauses. The number changes from 60 to 55, not from 60 to 10, because the new fact is real but not huge. The team can see the move. Nobody has to pretend the old answer was perfect.

The first answer is a suspect, not a pet. It keeps judgment from turning into a costume. A person can sound brave while hiding from the record. A quieter person with dates, odds, and reviews may be doing the harder thing.

The limit matters. Long-range shocks, hidden incentives, and fragile systems can make even careful work miss. A good forecaster does not use that as an excuse to blur every claim. She uses it to sort questions. Some deserve a wide range. Some deserve a backup plan. Some deserve no forecast stronger than a shrug.

Try the move on a live claim today. Take one future sentence you hear at work, at home, or in the news. Cut it into a smaller question. Put a probability on it. Write why you chose that number. Then mark the date when you will look again. The act takes two minutes. The habit changes the room because it makes confidence answerable.

examples.title: Ylva draws four boxes around the promotion bet

planSpec.audience: an HR lead forecasting a promotion outcome
planSpec.stakes: whether one smart hunch hides several subquestions
planSpec.requiredBeat: she decomposes a promotion forecast before advising the VP

examples.scenario: Ylva presses a ruler against a legal pad at 6:31 p.m. in the HR conference nook, drawing four boxes under the name of a manager up for promotion. The VP asked, will he succeed? Ylva's first answer is yes, easy. Then she labels the boxes: team retention, budget skill, peer trust, crisis judgment. The office cleaner is vacuuming by the glass wall. Ylva has to decide whether to send the quick yes or score the four smaller bets first.
examples.whatToDo: Score the subquestions before advising the VP. Give each box its own probability, then combine them into a recommendation with the weakest box visible.
examples.whyItMatters: A single yes hides where the risk lives. Smaller forecasts show which part of the promotion bet deserves support or doubt.

examples.title: Iskra splits the surgery backlog by ward

planSpec.stakes: whether an average hides the constraint that matters
planSpec.requiredBeat: she decomposes the backlog instead of trusting one total

examples.scenario: Iskra lifts a blue magnet from the surgery board at 9:50 a.m., its edge sticky from old tape. The chief wants to know whether the backlog clears by Friday. The total number says maybe. Iskra splits the list by surgeon, ward bed, and recovery nurse, then sees the answer change. Orthopedics can move. Cardiac cannot. Her coffee has gone cold while the average keeps lying politely from the top of the sheet.
examples.whatToDo: Break the backlog into bottlenecks. Forecast each constraint separately, then report the total with the tightest constraint named.
examples.whyItMatters: The total can look manageable while one ward breaks the plan. Decomposition finds the part that will decide the outcome.

examples.title: Bode opens last year’s camp ledger first

planSpec.audience: a camp director estimating summer enrollment
planSpec.stakes: whether enthusiasm beats the base rate
planSpec.requiredBeat: he uses last year’s comparable numbers before adjusting for new facts

examples.scenario: Bode unlocks the metal file cabinet at 7:43 a.m. in the rec center office, sunscreen smell still trapped in the old camp T-shirts. His gut says enrollment will jump because the new climbing wall looks great. Before he tells the board, he opens last year's ledger. Same early-bird week, same school calendar, 118 signups. This year shows 123. The climbing wall may help, but the base rate has already cooled the story.
examples.whatToDo: Start with last year's comparable signup curve. Adjust only for specific changes, like the climbing wall or bus route, and show the adjustment separately.
examples.whyItMatters: The base rate prevents excitement from becoming the whole forecast. It gives the new feature a fair amount of weight, not all the weight.

examples.title: Chandra asks what breaks the brilliant chess line

planSpec.audience: a coach reviewing a student's tournament forecast
planSpec.stakes: whether talent protects a favorite prediction from attack
planSpec.requiredBeat: she makes the student argue against his best line

examples.scenario: Chandra taps a black knight against the table at 11:07 p.m. in the chess club, where the vending machine hums through the wall. Her student says he is 80 percent to win Saturday if he reaches his favorite Sicilian line. "What ruins it?" Chandra asks. He smiles, then stops. "If Rowan trades queens early," he says. Chandra pushes the scoresheet toward him. "Write that probability too." He has to decide whether his favorite line survives its first enemy.
examples.whatToDo: Make the failure mode explicit. Forecast how often the opponent can force it, then lower the win estimate if that path is common.
examples.whyItMatters: Smart people protect elegant answers because the answers feel like part of them. Attacking the favorite line turns intelligence into testing instead of defense.

examples.title: Safiya sorts demand by bus route and school closure

planSpec.audience: a food-bank director estimating holiday demand
planSpec.stakes: whether one big demand number misses the families who arrive
planSpec.requiredBeat: she breaks demand into drivers and revises the order

examples.scenario: At 2:42 p.m., Safiya stands between pallets of rice in the food-bank warehouse, marker dust on her sleeve. Before, she ordered holiday boxes from one total: last year plus ten percent. Today she draws columns for family size, school closure, bus route, and freezer access. The west route jumps. The east route holds. By Friday the new order looks uneven, which makes the volunteers nervous, until the west line stretches around the block and the extra boxes land where they are needed.
examples.whatToDo: Build the demand estimate from drivers, not from one blanket increase. Let each driver change the order where it applies.
examples.whyItMatters: A complex need rarely grows evenly. The parts show where extra help belongs, which a single percentage cannot see.

examples.title: Gethin marks the bridge estimate he loved too much

planSpec.audience: an engineer reviewing a repair-cost miss
planSpec.stakes: whether expertise protects a cherished first estimate
planSpec.requiredBeat: he finds the subquestion he skipped because the first estimate felt elegant

examples.scenario: Gethin sits in the trailer at 8:06 p.m., rain ticking on the roof, the bridge repair invoice spread beside a muddy boot print. His first estimate missed by a third. He had nailed the steel cost and guessed the river-access cost from memory. Now the crane rental line glares up at him. He can blame the flood stage, but the gauge history was available. He has to decide whether the next estimate gets a river-access subquestion every time.
examples.whatToDo: Add the skipped subquestion to the estimating checklist. Price river access from gauge history before touching the total.
examples.whyItMatters: Expertise failed where it stopped looking. A checklist for the weak subquestion turns a painful miss into a better next estimate.

questions.prompt: A manager at 8:10 a.m. hears a polished forecast for a complex decision but sees no written odds or date. Which move best fits the skill of breaking problems into parts?
choices: Write a dated probability and ask what result would count as a miss.
Trust the confident speaker because clear delivery usually means better judgment.
Wait for perfect proof and refuse to act until uncertainty disappears.

reviewCards.front: You hear a confident claim about a complex decision. What do you ask before trusting it?
reviewCards.back: Ask for the dated probability, the base rate, and the outcome that would count as a miss. Forecasts improve when they can be checked, not when they sound smooth.

reviewCards.front: A fresh story makes your estimate feel wrong. How should you update?
reviewCards.back: Move the odds by the strength of the new evidence. A vivid story can matter, but it should not erase the older record unless it directly changes the facts.

reviewCards.front: A team wants one bold answer. What smaller move protects learning?
reviewCards.back: Break the issue into dated subquestions. Smaller forecasts show which assumption failed, so the next estimate can improve instead of becoming a blame session.

reviewCards.front: A miss is embarrassing. What should the review preserve?
reviewCards.back: Keep the original wording and number. Then mark which assumption failed. The record has to sting a little or it will not teach.

implementationPlan.coreSkill: The core skill is cutting a hard question into smaller pieces that can be checked and challenged. Practice means writing the claim before the outcome arrives, then updating it in small, visible steps. The point is not to look cautious. The point is to give reality a way to train you.

ifThenPlans.plan: If a work meeting turns on a complex decision, then write one dated probability on the agenda and name the result that would prove it wrong.
If you are choosing a health step under uncertainty, then write the base rate you know, the personal fact that changes it, and the next check-in date.
If a personal plan depends on a guess, then split the guess into one small forecast you can check within seven days.
If someone you care about sounds certain about the future, then ask what evidence would make both of you lower the odds by ten points.

implementationPlan.twentyFourHourChallenge: Before tomorrow night, write one live forecast about a complex decision with a date, a probability, and two reasons for the number. Put a reminder on the date to check it without rewriting the original line.
implementationPlan.weeklyPractice: Once this week, review one old forecast before you know the outcome. Move the number only if new evidence deserves it, and write the reason in one sentence.
